newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: First ladies press for rights of women and children.
newsitem.headline: First ladies press for rights of women and children.

text.p: Hillary Rodham Clinton and other first ladies from all over the Americas launched a drive on Tuesday to foster women's and children's rights, combat family violence and give women more participation in public life.
"Democracy requires the participation of all citizens, including women," Clinton told the opening session of the sixth conference of first ladies of the Americas.
Bolivia's first lady Ximena Iturralde-Sanchez, who is hosting the four-day meeting, demanded concrete steps so that "women have equal access to positions of power."

The conference, entitled "The rights of women and children within the framework of sustainable human development," runs until Friday. It will be followed immediately by a weekend hemispheric summit on sustainable development in Santa Cruz, 300 miles (500 km) southeast of La Paz.
On the opening day of the meeting, the first ladies demanded better access to health and education for women and children and legislation to protect them from abuse at home.
Clinton argued that better access to schooling should also help bring down the number of deaths from illegal abortions. "Education is closely related to abortion," she said.

On her first visit to Bolivia, one of Latin America's poorest nations, she visited the Andean peak of La Cumbre, just outside La Paz, and stopped at a street market to talk to women fruit vendors clad in typical Colla indian outfits and be pictured with children. The country's population is largely aborigine.
Accompanied by the Bolivian first lady, Clinton also visited a health centre and a cooperative bank specialising in credits for the poor and talked to patients and loan beneficiaries.
Outside the bank, which makes loans of as little as $100, she stopped to listen to a group of youngsters play Andean music.

During her two-day visit, she also plans to participate in a signing ceremony of a U.S. Agency for International Development grant to the Pan-American Health Organisation to pursue maternal mortality education in Latin America.

The Santa Cruz summit on sustainable development will be attended by more than 20 Latin American leaders and by U.S. Vice President Al Gore, who has had a longstanding interest in environmental issues.

Sustainable development, a principle approved by world leaders at the "Earth Summit" in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in 1992, is generally defined as pursuing economic growth without harming the environment.

The presidential summit will deal with a range of issues linked to sustainable development, including poverty, education, wider public participation in development projects, funding, and environmentally clean technology.
